summary: Describes a general mechanism that lets other protocols derive their own keying material from a TLS session, after TLS has done the key establishment. This avoids reinventing key exchange. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Once two computers share a secret, a clever trick can turn that one secret into new, different secrets for other jobs. This document defines that trick for TLS.

questions: what are tls keying material exporters
how to derive keys from a tls session
subtitle: How a TLS session can hand out fresh, independent keys to the protocols that ride on top of it.

tldr.problem: Some protocols use TLS or DTLS to establish keys but then want to use part of the keying material for their own purposes, such as DTLS-SRTP generating SRTP keys.
tldr.mechanism: An exporter takes a label, an optional context value and a length, and runs the TLS pseudorandom function (PRF) over the master_secret and the two hello randoms to produce that many bytes of keying material.
tldr.outcome: Different labels give independent values, so one session can serve many purposes. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8446, RFC 8447 and RFC 9846.

today: RFC 5705 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010, and it has been updated by RFC 8446, RFC 8447 and RFC 9846. Read those updates together with this document.

sections.title: Why Export Keys From TLS
sections.content:
A number of protocols want to use Transport Layer Security (TLS) or Datagram TLS (DTLS) to do key establishment, and then use some of the keying material for their own purposes. The RFC's typical example is DTLS-SRTP, which uses DTLS to perform a key exchange and negotiate the SRTP protection suite, and then uses the DTLS master_secret to generate the SRTP keys.

The RFC calls the output Exported Keying Material (EKM). It notes that the mechanism was previously known as "TLS Extractors" and was renamed to avoid a name clash with the cryptographic term "Extractor". It is compatible with all versions of TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two friends who share a secret handshake. This document lets them use that handshake to invent new secret handshakes for other games.

sections.title: What an Exporter Must Provide
sections.content:
The RFC lists four requirements for the mechanism:

  • Both client and server need to be able to export the same EKM value.
  • EKM values should be indistinguishable from random data to attackers who do not know the master_secret.
  • It should be possible to export multiple EKM values from the same TLS/DTLS association.
  • Knowing one EKM value should not reveal any useful information about the master_secret or about other EKM values.
sections.plainLanguage: Both friends must end up with the same new secret, it must look like random noise to outsiders, and learning one new secret must not help anyone guess the others.

sections.title: Binding Keys to an Application Context
sections.content:
Getting keys out of TLS is only half of the job. The application also has to securely agree on the upper-layer context where the keys will be used, for example the algorithms and parameters, the identifiers of the endpoints and sessions, and the lifetimes. At a minimum there should be some way to signal that an exporter will be used.

The RFC does not mandate one mechanism. It gives three examples that can complement each other:

  • Put context information in the optional data after the exporter label.
  • Exchange it in TLS extensions in the ClientHello and ServerHello messages, as DTLS-SRTP does. The Finished messages protect the handshake, so both peers end up with the same view.
  • Let the upper-layer protocol run its own handshake, protected by the exported keys.

However it is agreed, one part must say which application will use the exported keys: the disambiguating label string. Simply embedding TLS messages in an upper-layer protocol may not secure the context, because those upper-layer messages are not covered by the TLS Finished messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Having a new secret is not enough. Both friends must also agree what game it is for, and they must agree in a way a cheater cannot change.

sections.title: The Exporter Definition
sections.content:
An exporter takes three inputs: a disambiguating label string, a per-association context value supplied by the application, and a length. The output is a pseudorandom bit string of length bytes generated from the master_secret, and it is meant to be used in a single scope tied to the TLS session, the label and the context value.

With no context, the exporter computes the TLS PRF over the master secret, the label, and the client and server random values joined together. With a context, it also appends the context value length and the context value. This construction keeps the no-context form interoperable with older exporter-type constructions such as the one in RFC 5281.

Labels are ASCII strings with no terminating NULL. Labels beginning with EXPERIMENTAL MAY be used privately without registration. All other labels MUST be registered via Specification Required. To avoid collisions with existing PRF labels, labels SHOULD begin with EXPORTER, which is not a MUST because some existing uses do not follow that prefix.

The context value lets the application mix its own data into the output. The RFC's example is an authentication setting where client credentials are valid for more than one identity: mixing the expected identity into the keying material prevents substitution attacks. The context length is a 16-bit unsigned value and the context MAY be zero length.
sections.plainLanguage: You mix the shared secret with a name for the job (the label) and some extra details (the context). Change the name and you get a completely different new secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The prime requirement is that exporter outputs are independent. Even if an attacker chooses several (label, context value) pairs and sees the outputs, it must not be able to tell the output for a different pair from a random value of the same length. An attacker who controls the context value MUST NOT be able to predict the exporter output. The current TLS PRFs are believed to meet this, provided the master secret is randomly generated.

Because the same label applied to the same master secret gives the same value, two EKM values made with the same label must not be used for two different purposes. That is why labels are registered. Revealing an EKM value made from one label is not a threat to values made from another label.

With certain cipher suites the master secret is not necessarily unique to one session. With RSA key exchange, a malicious party acting as TLS server in one session and TLS client in another can make the two sessions share a master secret, though the sessions must be set up simultaneously. Applications need to consider this, and requiring cipher suites that use Diffie-Hellman key exchange may be advisable. The RFC also warns that designing a secure mechanism that uses exporters is not necessarily straightforward, and that new uses should be carefully reviewed.
sections.plainLanguage: Different job names must give secrets that look unrelated. Also, a sneaky middleman in some setups could make two chats share one secret, so apps should be careful.

sections.title: The Exporter Label Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a TLS Exporter Label registry. Its initial contents are client finished, server finished, master secret and key expansion (reserved, because they are used for a similar but distinct purpose in RFC 5246 and MUST NOT be used for exporters), plus client EAP encryption (RFC 5216), ttls keying material and ttls challenge (RFC 5281).

Future values are allocated under the Specification Required policy. A label is a string of printable ASCII characters, and IANA MUST also verify that no label is a prefix of any other label. For example, key and master secretary are forbidden.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a public list of job names so nobody uses the same name for two different jobs. No name may be the beginning of another name.

viz.caption: THE EXPORTER WITH A CONTEXT VALUE (RFC 5705, SECTION 4)

data.title: Exporter with context
data.code:
PRF(SecurityParameters.master_secret, label,
    SecurityParameters.client_random +
    SecurityParameters.server_random +
    context_value_length + context_value
    )[length]
